definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Attendance on the teacher (ācārya-upāsana) is among the items called knowledge (13.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.8: among the dispositions called knowledge.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.12: constancy in knowledge of what pertains to the self is among the dispositions called knowledge; 15.5: those constantly intent on it (adhyātmanitya) go to the imperishable place.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The sense of 'I', listed among the constituents of the field (13.6); its absence (anahaṃkāra) is among the items called knowledge (13.9).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Non-harming, among the items called knowledge (13.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: what differs from the dispositions called knowledge is ignorance (13.12); tamas is born of ignorance (14.8); ignorance is the fruit of tamas and arises from it (14.16–17).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Space: all-pervading and, because of its subtlety, unstained, as the self present in the body is unstained (13.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.16: of the two persons in the world, the one standing firm (kūṭastha) is called the imperishable; Kṛṣṇa is higher even than the imperishable (15.18). What the akṣara denotes here is read differently by the commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Indolence, one of the three by which tamas binds (14.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.8: the first of the dispositions called knowledge.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.13: knowing the knowable one attains the immortal; 14.20: the embodied one who goes beyond the three guṇas attains it; 14.27: Kṛṣṇa is the foundation of the imperishable immortal.

Bhagavad Gītā 15.7: 'a portion of me indeed, eternal, having become the living being in the world of the living' draws the senses with the mind. The sense of 'portion' is read differently by the commentators.

Bhagavad Gītā 13.11: 'unswerving devotion (bhakti avyabhicāriṇī) to me through a yoga that has no other (ananya-yoga)' is among the dispositions called knowledge; compare 14.26 (avyabhicāra bhakti-yoga).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.23: one of the names of 'the highest puruṣa in this body'.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Joined with prāṇa and apāna, the Lord as vaiśvānara digests the fourfold food (15.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 15.15: from Kṛṣṇa, seated in the heart of all, come memory, knowledge and apohana — taken by most commentators as their loss, by some as reasoning.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Undertaking: the undertaking of actions is a sign of rajas (14.12); the one beyond the guṇas has given up all undertakings (14.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Uprightness, among the items called knowledge (13.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: non-attachment (asakti, the abstract noun) is among the dispositions called knowledge (13.10); the knowable is unattached (asaktam), yet supports all (13.15). Not to be confused with aśakti, 'incapacity' (trm:asakti).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.13: brahman, beginningless and supreme, is said to be neither sat nor asat.

Bhagavad Gītā 15.1–3: the imperishable aśvattha is spoken of with roots above and branches below, its leaves the metres; one who knows it knows the Veda; its branches spread below and above, swollen by the guṇas, with the sense-objects as shoots, and its roots below are bound up with action in the human world; its form, end, beginning and foundation are not perceived here; it is to be cut with the weapon of non-attachment.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Read reflexively in ātma-vinigraha, 'restraint of oneself' (13.8), in 'in themselves, by themselves' (13.25), in 'does not harm oneself by oneself' (13.29), in 'praise of oneself' (14.24) and in 'abiding in themselves' (15.11); as 'the self' in 13.25 (ātmānam) and 13.33, where the self present in the body is unstained like space; the supreme self is paramātman (13.23, 13.32, 15.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.8: among the dispositions called knowledge (the compound is reflexive: restraint of oneself).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.6: listed among the constituents of the field, after the great elements, ahaṅkāra and buddhi.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Imperishable: said of the embodied one (14.5), the supreme self (13.32), the aśvattha (15.1), the place reached by the undeluded (15.5) and the lord who sustains the three worlds (15.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord's devotee who understands the field, knowledge and the knowable comes to the Lord's state (13.19).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Unswerving devotion to the Lord is counted among the items called knowledge (13.11); unswerving bhakti-yoga carries one beyond the guṇas (14.26); whoever knows the Lord as the highest person worships (bhajati) him with his whole being (15.19).
Bhagavad Gītā 14.26: one who serves Kṛṣṇa with the unswerving yoga of devotion, having gone beyond the guṇas, becomes fit for becoming brahman.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the knowable is without guṇas yet their experiencer (guṇabhoktṛ, 13.15); puruṣa is the cause in the experiencing (bhoktṛtva) of pleasure and pain (13.21) and, situated in prakṛti, experiences the guṇas (13.22); 'experiencer' is among the names of the highest puruṣa in the body (13.23).
Bhagavad Gītā 14.4: Kṛṣṇa is the seed-giving father (bījaprada pitā) of all forms, the great brahman their womb.
Bhagavad Gītā 14.26: one who serves Kṛṣṇa with the unswerving yoga of devotion, having gone beyond the guṇas, becomes fit for becoming brahman (brahmabhūyāya kalpate; the phrase recurs at 18.53).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the knowable is brahman, beginningless and supreme, said to be neither sat nor asat (13.13), described in 13.14–18; one who sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the one and spreading from it attains brahman (13.31); by unswerving devotion one becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); Kṛṣṇa is the foundation (pratiṣṭhā) of brahman (14.27). In 14.3–4 'the great brahman' is Kṛṣṇa's womb (see mahad brahma).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.6: listed among the constituents of the field; 15.20: understanding this teaching one becomes possessed of buddhi (buddhimat).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.7: listed among the constituents of the field (with desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate and steadiness) — i.e. on the side of the field, not of its knower.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Thought: those who have not formed themselves and lack thought (acetas) do not see the one abiding in themselves, even though they strive (15.11).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The metres (or the hymns in them): the field and its knower have been sung in them (13.5); they are the leaves of the aśvattha (15.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Evenness of thought (sama-cittatva) amid the desired and the undesired is among the items called knowledge (13.10).

literal: mind; that which is conscious (as if)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the highest puruṣa is 'in this body' (13.23); the self present everywhere in the body is not stained (13.33); the guṇas bind the imperishable embodied one in the body (14.5); illumination at all the gates of this body shows that sattva has increased (14.11); the Lord as vaiśvānara dwells in the bodies of breathing beings (15.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the guṇas bind the imperishable embodied one in the body (14.5, 14.7); the embodied one who goes beyond the three guṇas attains the immortal (14.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord is the foundation of everlasting (śāśvata) dharma (14.27).

literal: that which upholds; right order, duty

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Steadfast: a mark of the one beyond the guṇas (14.24).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.7: listed among the constituents of the field.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Meditation: by it some see the self in themselves by themselves (13.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 14.19: when the seer beholds no agent other than the guṇas and knows what is beyond them, he attains Kṛṣṇa's state.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: pain is listed among the contents of the field (13.7); keeping in view the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness and pain is counted as knowledge (13.9); puruṣa is the cause in the experiencing of pleasure and pain (13.21); pain is the fruit of rajas (14.16); going beyond the guṇas the embodied one is freed from birth, death, old age and pain (14.20); the one gone beyond them is alike in pain and pleasure (14.24); the undeluded are released from the pairs known as pleasure and pain (15.5).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The pairs known as pleasure and pain, released from which the undeluded reach the imperishable place (15.5).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Aversion, listed among the contents of the field (13.7); the one beyond the guṇas does not hate illumination, activity and delusion when they are present (14.22).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The teaching on the highest person is called the most secret teaching (guhyatama śāstra) (15.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20, 14.5); puruṣa experiences them and attachment to them causes birth (13.22); the knowable is without guṇas yet their experiencer (13.15). Chapter 14: the three guṇas — sattva, rajas and tamas — bind the embodied one (14.5–9), prevail by overpowering one another (14.10), show their signs (14.11–13), shape what follows death (14.14–15, 14.18) and the fruit of action (14.16–17); one who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains Kṛṣṇa's state (14.19); the embodied one who goes beyond them attains the immortal (14.20). The aśvattha's branches are swollen by the guṇas (15.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 14.20–26: the embodied one who goes beyond the three guṇas attains the immortal, freed from birth, death, old age and pain (14.20). Asked for his marks, conduct and means (14.21): he does not hate illumination, activity or delusion when they arise nor long for them when they cease; sitting as one indifferent he is not shaken by the guṇas, knowing 'the guṇas operate'; he is the same in pleasure and pain, toward clod, stone and gold, the pleasant and unpleasant, blame and praise, honour and dishonour, friend and foe, and relinquishes all undertakings — he is called guṇātīta (14.22–25); one who serves Kṛṣṇa with unswerving devotion goes beyond the guṇas (14.26).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: prakṛti is said to be the cause (hetu) in agency, puruṣa the cause in experiencing (13.21); the brahmasūtra words are 'furnished with reasons' (hetumat) (13.5).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The heart: the knowable is seated in the heart of all (13.18); the Lord is seated in the heart of all (15.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Desire, listed first among the states that belong to the field (13.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the ten senses 'and the one' belong to the field (13.6); the knowable appears through the qualities of all the senses yet is devoid of them (13.15); the portion of Kṛṣṇa that has become the living being draws the senses with the mind as sixth, which abide in prakṛti, carries them from body to body, and presiding over ear, eye, touch, taste, smell and mind enjoys objects (15.7–9).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Dispassion toward the objects of the senses is among the items called knowledge (13.9).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: seeing the lord equally present everywhere one does not harm oneself (13.29); in 15.8 the living being of 15.7 is called īśvara as it takes up and leaves a body; the highest person is the imperishable lord who enters and sustains the three worlds (15.17).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.7: an eternal portion of Kṛṣṇa, become the living being (jīvabhūta) in the world of the living, draws the senses; 15.8–11 describe it taking a body, leaving it, enjoying objects, seen only by those with the eye of knowledge.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The world of the living, in which the Lord's portion becomes the living being (15.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: (1) the knowledge of the field and its knower is knowledge in Kṛṣṇa's view (13.3); (2) twenty dispositions, from absence of pride to keeping in view the aim of knowledge of reality, are declared knowledge, and what differs from them ignorance (13.8–12); (3) the knowable is itself called knowledge (13.18); (4) the highest knowledge by which the sages reached perfection (14.1–2); (5) sattva binds by attachment to knowledge and knowledge arises from sattva; tamas covers it (14.6, 14.9, 14.11, 14.17); (6) it comes, with memory and removal (apohana), from Kṛṣṇa (15.15).

Bhagavad Gītā 13.35: with the eye of knowledge one knows the difference between the field and its knower; 15.10: the deluded do not see the living being departing, staying or enjoying, those with the eye of knowledge see it.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: one of the topics Arjuna asks about (13.1). The knowable is brahman, beginningless and supreme, knowing which one attains the immortal, said to be neither sat nor asat (13.13); it has hands, feet, eyes everywhere, appears through the sense-qualities yet is without senses, is without guṇas yet their experiencer, is inside and outside beings, not to be known because of its subtlety, undivided yet as if divided, sustainer, devourer and generator of beings (13.14–17); light of lights beyond darkness, it is knowledge, the knowable and what is reached by knowledge, set in the heart of all (13.18). Knowing it, the devotee becomes fit for Kṛṣṇa's state (13.19).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The knowable is the light even of lights, beyond darkness (13.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Those whose desires have turned away (vinivṛtta-kāma) reach the imperishable place (15.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Actions are done in every way by prakṛti alone (13.30); rajas binds by attachment to action (14.7, 14.9); the fruit of well-done action is sāttvika and stainless (14.16); the aśvattha's roots bind through action (15.2).

literal: action; ritual act; the deed and its result

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The yoga of action: one of the means by which the self is seen (13.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.30: one who sees actions done by prakṛti alone and his self as not the doer (akartṛ) sees; 14.19: the seer beholds no agent other than the guṇas.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.21: prakṛti is said to be the cause in the agency regarding effects and instruments (kārya-kāraṇa).

literal: one who has done what is to be done

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 15.20: understanding this most secret teaching one becomes wise and kṛtakṛtya.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Forbearance, among the items called knowledge (13.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 15.16: of the two persons in the world, the perishable is 'all beings'; Kṛṣṇa is beyond the perishable (15.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the body (śarīra) is called the field (13.2). In brief it consists of the great elements, ahaṅkāra, buddhi, the unmanifest, the ten senses and the one, the five ranges of the senses, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience (cetanā) and steadiness, together with its modifications (13.6–7). Every being is born from the union of field and knower (13.27); the possessor of the field illumines the whole field as the sun the world (13.34); knowing the difference between field and knower leads to the supreme (13.35).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the one who knows the body-field is called by those who know it the knower of the field (13.2); Kṛṣṇa says 'know me also as the knower of the field in all fields', and the knowledge of field and knower is knowledge (13.3); beings are born from the union of field and knower (13.27); their difference is known with the eye of knowledge (13.35). How 13.3 relates Kṛṣṇa to the individual knower is read differently by the commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.34: the one who has the field; as the one sun illumines this whole world, so the kṣetrin illumines the whole field. Used for the knower of the field.
Bhagavad Gītā 15.16: the imperishable (akṣara) puruṣa is called the one standing firm (kūṭastha).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Arjuna asks by what marks (liṅgaiḥ) the one gone beyond the three guṇas is known (14.21); the marks are given in 14.22–25.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Greed: a sign and a product of rajas (14.12, 14.17).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: dying when sattva has increased, one reaches the stainless worlds (lokān) of those who know the highest (14.14); there are two puruṣas in the world (loke) (15.16); the highest person enters and sustains the three worlds (loka-traya) (15.17); he is renowned 'in the world and in the Veda' as puruṣottama (15.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 13.19: Kṛṣṇa's devotee, knowing the field, knowledge and the knowable, becomes fit for his state; 14.19: the seer who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains it.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.6: the great elements head the list of the field's constituents.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'Great brahman' (mahad brahma): the Lord's womb, in which he places the germ from which all beings come (14.3-14.4).

notes: Chs. 13–15 contribution, merged from extractor B's trm:mahat and extractor A's new trm:mahad-brahma (mapped here: data/ already records the Gītā's 'great brahman' under trm:mahat). The commentators identify this 'great brahman' with prakṛti; the text does not use that word here, and it is not the Sāṃkhya mahat (the first evolute).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 15.7–9: the senses 'with the mind as the sixth' are drawn by the living being, taken along at death, and presided over in enjoying objects. (The 'one' after the ten senses in 13.6 is taken by the commentators as manas.)

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Delusion: tamas deludes all embodied beings (14.8); delusion is a sign and product of tamas (14.13, 14.17); the one beyond the guṇas does not hate it when present (14.22); the undeluded reach the imperishable place and know the Lord as the highest person (15.5, 15.19); the deluded do not see the living being (15.10).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Release: those who know the difference of field and knower and the release from the prakṛti of beings (bhūta-prakṛti-mokṣa) go to the highest (13.35).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: keeping in view the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness and pain is counted as knowledge (13.9); those who worship having heard from others cross beyond death (13.26); going beyond the three guṇas the embodied one is freed from birth, death, old age and pain (14.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The sages who, by the highest knowledge, went from here to the highest perfection (14.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Sleep, one of the three by which tamas binds (14.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the knowable is without guṇas yet their experiencer (13.15); the supreme self, being beginningless and without guṇas, neither acts nor is tainted though in the body (13.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Vigour: entering the earth, the Lord sustains beings by his vigour (15.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The place: to be sought after cutting the aśvattha, from which those who reach it do not return (15.4); the imperishable place reached by the undeluded (15.5).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord's supreme abode, which neither sun nor moon nor fire illumines, and from which those who reach it do not return (15.6).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: one of the names of 'the highest puruṣa in this body' (13.23); this supreme self, beginningless, without guṇas and imperishable, though dwelling in the body neither acts nor is tainted (13.32); the highest person, other than the perishable and the imperishable, is called the supreme self, the imperishable lord who enters and sustains the three worlds (15.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.28: one who sees the supreme lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing among the perishing, sees.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Light, illumination: sattva is illuminating (14.6); the light of knowledge in all the gates of the body shows that sattva has increased (14.11); absence of light is a sign of tamas (14.13); the one beyond the guṇas does not hate illumination when present (14.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; the modifications and the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20); it is the cause in the agency regarding effects and instruments (13.21); puruṣa situated in it experiences the guṇas born of it (13.22); actions are done in every way by prakṛti alone (13.30); the three guṇas arise from it (14.5); the senses with mind abide in it (15.7). 13.35 speaks of release from the prakṛti of beings.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Dissolution: those who have come to sameness of nature with the Lord are not troubled at dissolution (14.2); the word also names death, the dissolution of the embodied one (14.14-14.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: tamas binds by heedlessness, idleness and sleep (14.8) and attaches to heedlessness (14.9); heedlessness arises when tamas increases and comes from it (14.13, 14.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Joined with prāṇa and apāna, the Lord as vaiśvānara digests the fourfold food (15.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'I take refuge (prapadye) in that very primal person from whom the ancient stream of activity flowed forth' — the words with which the place of no return is sought (15.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Foundation: the Lord is the foundation of brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of everlasting dharma and of absolute happiness (14.27); the foundation (saṃpratiṣṭhā) of the aśvattha is not perceived (15.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Activity: a sign of rajas (14.12), its absence a sign of tamas (14.13); the one beyond the guṇas neither hates it nor longs for it (14.22); the ancient stream of activity flowed forth from the primal person (15.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: puruṣa and prakṛti are both beginningless (13.20); puruṣa is the cause in the experiencing of pleasure and pain (13.21); situated in prakṛti it experiences the guṇas, and attachment to them causes its births (13.22); 'the highest puruṣa in this body' is called onlooker, consenter, supporter, experiencer, great lord and supreme self (13.23); one who knows puruṣa and prakṛti is not born again (13.24). In chapter 15 there are two puruṣas in the world, the perishable and the imperishable (15.16), and the highest puruṣa, another (15.17); Kṛṣṇa is the puruṣottama (15.18); one takes refuge in the primal puruṣa (15.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.18–19: because Kṛṣṇa is beyond the perishable and higher even than the imperishable, he is renowned in the world and in the Veda as the puruṣottama; one who undeluded knows him so knows all and worships him with his whole being. 15.17 calls the highest person (uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ) the supreme self and imperishable lord.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Passion: the nature of rajas (14.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: rajas is of the nature of passion, bound up with the arising of thirst and attachment; it binds by attachment to action (14.7) and attaches to action (14.9); when it increases, greed, activity, undertaking of actions, restlessness and craving arise (14.12); dying in it one is born among those attached to action (14.15); its fruit is pain (14.16); greed arises from it (14.17); the rājasa remain in the middle (14.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The seers have sung of the field and its knower in many ways (13.5).

literal: having the same nature or properties

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 14.2: resorting to the highest knowledge, the sages have come to sādharmya with Kṛṣṇa and are not born at creation nor troubled at dissolution.

notes: Śaṅkara: identity with the Lord's nature; Rāmānuja: likeness of attributes.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Evenness: constant evenness of thought (sama-cittatva) amid the desired and the undesired (13.10); the one beyond the guṇas is the same in pain and pleasure, toward clod, stone and gold, in blame and praise, honour and dishonour (14.24-14.25); the Lord is seen abiding equally (samam) in all beings (13.28-13.29).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.25: some see the self by the yoga of sāṃkhya (sāṃkhyena yogena), as others by meditation or by karma-yoga.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Union: every being, stationary or moving, arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field (13.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Eternal: said of the Lord's portion that becomes the living being (15.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Attachment: attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs (13.22); sattva binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action (14.6-14.7); non-attachment (asaṅga) is the weapon that cuts the aśvattha (15.3); the fault of attachment is to be conquered (15.5).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.7: listed among the constituents of the field.

notes: The commentators take it as the aggregate of body and organs.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Creation: those who have come to sameness of nature with the Lord are not born even at creation (14.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: this body is called the field (13.2); the supreme self, though dwelling in the body (śarīra-stha), neither acts nor is stained (13.32); the living being takes up a body and departs from it, taking the senses and mind with it (15.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: All-pervading: said of space in the simile for the unstained self (13.33).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.13: brahman, beginningless and supreme, is said to be neither sat nor asat.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: sattva, being stainless, is illuminating and free of affliction; it binds by attachment to happiness and to knowledge (14.6), attaches to happiness (14.9); when illumination-knowledge arises at all the gates of the body it has increased (14.11); dying in it one reaches the stainless worlds of the knowers of the highest (14.14); knowledge arises from it (14.17); those abiding in it go upward (14.18). In 13.27 'sattva' means simply 'a being'.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Purity, among the items called knowledge (13.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Perfection, attainment: the highest perfection (parā siddhi) to which the sages went by the highest knowledge (14.1) — here the goal, not a yogic power.
Bhagavad Gītā 15.15: memory, knowledge and removal (apohana) come from Kṛṣṇa, seated in the heart of all.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Becoming soma, whose nature is sap, the Lord nourishes all plants (15.13); the commentators take soma here as the moon.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'What is heard': those who worship having heard from others, holding to what they have heard (śruti-parāyaṇa), also cross beyond death (13.26).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Happiness, pleasure: listed among the contents of the field (13.7); puruṣa is the cause in experiencing pleasure and pain (13.21); sattva binds by attachment to happiness (14.6, 14.9); the Lord is the foundation of absolute happiness (14.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 14.24: the one gone beyond the guṇas is svastha, alike in pain and pleasure.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: tamas is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings; it binds by heedlessness, idleness and sleep (14.8); covering knowledge it attaches to heedlessness (14.9); when it increases, absence of illumination, inactivity, heedlessness and delusion arise (14.13); dying in it one is born in deluded wombs (14.15); its fruit is ignorance (14.16); heedlessness, delusion and ignorance come from it (14.17); the tāmasa go downward (14.18). In 13.18 'tamas' is darkness (the knowable is beyond darkness).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.12: keeping in view the aim (artha) of the knowledge of reality is the last of the dispositions called knowledge.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Radiance: the radiance in the sun, the moon and fire is the Lord's (15.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Thirst: rajas is bound up with thirst and attachment (14.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 14.23: the one gone beyond the guṇas sits as one indifferent (udāsīnavat), not shaken by the guṇas.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.23: first of the names of 'the highest puruṣa in this body' (with consenter, supporter, experiencer, great lord, supreme self).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.26: others, not knowing this, worship (upāsate) having heard from others, and they too cross death.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Dispassion toward the objects of the senses, among the items called knowledge (13.9).
Bhagavad Gītā 15.14: becoming Vaiśvānara, dwelling in the bodies of breathing beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna, Kṛṣṇa digests the fourfold food.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Who knows the aśvattha knows the Veda (15.1); the Lord is what all the Vedas make known, the maker of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda (15.15); he is celebrated in the Veda as the highest person (15.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the field's modifications are among what is to be told (13.4); the field is described 'with its modifications' (13.7); the modifications and the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Sense-objects: the shoots of the aśvattha's branches (15.2); the living being, presiding over the senses and the mind, partakes of them (15.9).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: sickness is among the evils of birth, death, old age, sickness and pain, keeping which in view is counted as knowledge (13.9).

literal: yoking; (from yuj 'to concentrate', per Vyāsa and Bhoja) concentration

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: unswerving devotion to the Lord is 'through a yoga that has no other' (ananya-yoga) (13.11); some see the self by the yoga of sāṃkhya, others by the yoga of action (karma-yoga) (13.25); compare bhakti-yoga (14.26).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Yogins who strive see the one abiding in themselves (15.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs (13.22); the great brahman is Kṛṣṇa's womb and the womb of all forms (14.3–4); dying in tamas one is born in deluded wombs (14.15).
